title: The Broken Game
tagline: Four bugs. One broken game. You're the bug detectives.
objectives: I can read someone else's code and work out what it's supposed to do.
I can find a bug by testing, predicting and checking — not guessing randomly.
I can explain in my own words what was wrong and how I fixed it.

config.headline: Every game ever made went on sale with bugs in it.
lines: In 1947, one of the very first computers in the world stopped working. The engineers searched the machine for the **fault** — and found a real moth stuck inside it! They taped the moth into their logbook and wrote: 'First actual case of bug being found.'

Bugs never went away. Ever since, a **BUG** has meant a **mistake in a program**. Every game you have ever played had hundreds of them while it was being made. A team found them, one by one, so they could be fixed before the game went on sale. That team is called **QA**, short for **Quality Assurance**: checking a game really works before players get it. QA testing is a real job — and today it is yours.

In this lesson you will learn to **READ** code someone else wrote and work out what it is **SUPPOSED** to do. Then you will find what is actually wrong — by testing, predicting and checking, never by guessing. Those three skills are what this hour is for.

Last night, a games company called **OLS GAMES** released a new game: **Shark Attack**. This morning the players' reviews are terrible — four separate bugs got past the old testing team. You are the new QA team. Each complaint a player sends in is called a **TICKET**. The next screen is your CASE BOARD: all four tickets are pinned to it, waiting for you. Fix all four bugs and the players get their game back.

config.help: This screen is only for reading — it tells you what today's lesson is about. When the writing finishes, press the button at the bottom to start.

config.title: The Case Board
config.intro: Welcome to the QA team's Case Board. Each of the four player TICKETS you read about has been pinned up here, and each ticket has become a CASE: a folder holding one bug for you to find and fix. Start with the training case — it walks you through your first fix. After that, the other three cases open, and you can take them in any order you like. Every case is closed the same way:
config.introSolo: You are on your own today, so you do both jobs: you PLAY the game and you FIX the blocks. The four player TICKETS you read about are pinned up here, and each ticket has become a CASE: a folder holding one bug for you to find and fix. Start with the training case — it walks you through your first fix. After that, the other three cases open, and you can take them in any order. Every case is closed the same way:
config.pairNote: Work as a two-person detective agency with the pupil beside you: the PLAYER runs the game, reads the ticket out loud and says what they see; the ENGINEER moves the blocks. Swap jobs at every new case — a closed case belongs to both of you.

getgame.intro: A detective examines the REAL broken thing, not a photo of it. Get the broken game open on your own screen:

steps.title: Download the evidence
steps.text: Click the gold button — shark-attack-broken-edition.sb3 drops into your Downloads.

steps.title: Open the Scratch editor
steps.text: Use the second button — scratch.mit.edu opens in a new tab. No login needed, ever. Keep BOTH tabs open: case board here, game there.

steps.title: Load the broken game
steps.text: In Scratch, open the File menu and choose 'Load from your computer'. Pick shark-attack-broken-edition.sb3 from your Downloads, then press OK to replace.

steps.title: Walk the crime scene
steps.text: You should see a Shark, a Fish and a score stuck on 0. The little pictures at the bottom right are the game's SPRITES — a sprite is one character or thing in the game. Click a sprite and you will see its SCRIPTS: the stacks of blocks that tell that sprite what to do. Every sprite carries its OWN scripts, never anyone else's — that is why a bug can hide on one sprite while everything else looks fine. One more word you WILL meet on the Fish: CLONE. A clone is a temporary copy of a sprite that Scratch makes while the game runs — every fish swimming in the water is a clone of the one Fish sprite in the list. Most of the bugs are hiding in the sprites' scripts — but not all of them: one case will take you somewhere new.

getgame.confirm: The broken game is open in Scratch and I can see its code

handbook.title: Reading Someone Else's Code
handbook.fallback: If the film won't load, don't worry — your teacher's demonstration covers everything it shows, and the cards on this screen walk you through the rest.

cases.name: The Frozen Shark
cases.ticket: The shark won't swim RIGHT. Left, up, down — all fine. Right? Nothing. My shark just stares at the wall while the fish laugh at it. One star.
cases.symptom: Click the green flag to start the game, then press the RIGHT arrow key and watch what happens. Now try the other three arrow keys, one at a time. The player is not making it up.
cases.look: Open the Shark's scripts and compare them with each other. Working code is your best evidence: what does every WORKING arrow script start with that the broken one is missing? Cannot see all five stacks at once? Click the minus (–) button at the bottom right of the code area until they all fit.
cases.logHint: The right-arrow script had no… so I…
cases.replay: Click the green flag, then swim a full lap of the tank: RIGHT along the bottom, UP the far wall, LEFT across the top, DOWN back to where you started. Press all four arrow keys on the way round — no shortcuts.
cases.replayConfirm: Full lap swum — all four arrows work

clue.free: Re-read the ticket. Which arrows work? Which ONE doesn't? That tells you exactly which script to stare at.
clue.consult: Ask another agency — another detective pair — that has CLOSED Case 01. One question, detective to detective. (Your teacher also solved this one at the front.)
clue.consultSolo: No other agencies are on shift today — you are the whole QA team. If re-reading the ticket didn’t crack it, go straight to HQ’s clue below.
clue.hq: The bug lives on the SHARK. Put the four arrow-key scripts side by side and look at the very TOP of each.

mechanicSteps: The block at the very top of a stack is called a HAT BLOCK — it has a curved top, like a hat, and it is what starts the script running. A stack with no hat block never runs at all.
Click Events (the yellow group) and find 'when space key pressed'.
Drag it until it sits on top of the stack that has no hat — the right-arrow blocks. A white shadow line appears when it is about to snap on.
The new hat block says 'space'. Click that word and choose 'right arrow' from the list.

img.alt: A screenshot of the game: the shark pressed hard against the right-hand wall of the tank, with a fish swimming nearby.
img.caption: FinnTastic_11 sent this with the ticket: the shark stuck at the wall.

cases.name: The Broken Scoreboard
cases.ticket: I ate SO many fish — I kept restarting the game to eat more — and the score just sits on 0. I can literally HEAR the bite happen. This game is eating my points as well as the fish.
cases.symptom: Click the green flag and steer the shark to eat the fish. Listen for the bite sound… then look at the score. Click the flag again — a fresh fish arrives. Eat that one too. Still 0?
cases.look: Find the script that runs at the moment a fish gets eaten, and read it block by block, out loud. Every block will sound right — until you reach the one NUMBER that is wrong.
cases.logHint: The change-score block said… so I…
cases.replay: Click the green flag, eat the fish, and watch the score the moment you bite — it must jump to 1. Restart and prove it twice more. Right once could be luck; right three times is proof.
cases.replayConfirm: Three restarts, a clean point every time — the scoreboard tells the truth

clue.free: Re-read the ticket. The bite HAPPENS — the sound plays and the fish vanishes — so the eating part of the game works. What is the one thing that never moves?
clue.consult: Ask an agency that has CLOSED Case 02 — one question only, detective to detective. Nobody near you has closed it yet? Go straight to HQ’s clue below.
clue.consultSolo: No other agencies are on shift today — you are the whole QA team. If re-reading the ticket didn’t crack it, go straight to HQ’s clue below.
clue.hq: The bug lives on the FISH, in the script that starts 'when I start as a clone'.

img.alt: A screenshot of the game: the shark chasing a fish, with the score display in the corner still reading 0.
img.caption: ChompChamp07's screenshot: the hunt is on, and the score has not moved off 0.

mechanicSteps: Some scripts hold blocks you have not met yet — go to random position, glide, when I start as a clone. That is normal: real QA testers read code they did not write, every day.
You never need to understand every block. Read the stack out loud, and at each block ask: is this block’s job the thing the ticket says is broken? Skip every block whose job is something else.
To fix a wrong number: click the white oval on the block, type the right number, then press Enter. A number fix never moves a block.

cases.name: The Vanishing Fish
cases.ticket: One fish. ONE. I ate it in ten seconds flat and then swam round an empty ocean for the rest of my life. Where did everybody GO??
cases.symptom: Click the green flag, eat the first fish, then keep playing while you count slowly to ten. Watch the water the whole time: do any new fish arrive?
cases.look: One script's entire job is making new fish — each new fish is a CLONE, a temporary copy of the Fish sprite. Find that script and read it top to bottom: exactly how many times does it actually make one? One warning from HQ: the hide block at the very top is MEANT to be there. The Fish in the sprite list is only the mould — every swimming fish is a copy of it. The bug is about how many fish get MADE.
cases.logHint: The fish-maker script only ran… so I…
cases.replay: Click the green flag and play for twenty full seconds. Fish should KEEP arriving the whole time — count at least five new fish before you tick the stamp.
cases.replayConfirm: Fish kept coming the whole time

clue.free: Re-read the ticket. The FIRST fish was fine — it swam, it got eaten. It is everything AFTER that first fish the player never sees. So which script's whole job is making fish?
clue.consult: Ask an agency — another detective pair — that has already CLOSED Case 03. One question, so make it a good one. Nobody in the room has closed it yet? Skip this step and go straight to HQ’s clue below.
clue.consultSolo: No other agencies are on shift today — you are the whole QA team. If re-reading the ticket didn’t crack it, go straight to HQ’s clue below.
clue.hq: The bug lives on the FISH, in the script under 'when green flag clicked' (not the clone one).

mechanicSteps: Drag the blocks you want to repeat OUT onto an empty part of the code area first.
Drop a forever block under the hat block.
Drag your blocks back INSIDE the forever block's mouth — a white shadow line shows when they are about to land inside.

img.alt: A screenshot of the game: the whole tank of water with the shark alone in it and no fish anywhere.
img.caption: SharkSnackSara's screenshot: the whole ocean, empty.

cases.name: The White Void
cases.ticket: Every single time I press the green flag the sea DISAPPEARS. White screen, fish swimming in nothing, then the ocean strolls in a second late. It looks so broken I stopped playing.
cases.symptom: Click the green flag and watch ONLY the very first second. Then click it again. And again. Does the same wrong thing happen every time?
cases.look: This bug is not on a sprite at all — it is on the STAGE, the game's background. Click the Stage panel on the far right, beside the sprite list, to see its scripts. Read the script top to bottom, and at every block ask: what is the player SEEING right now?
cases.logHint: The script switched to… before… so I…
cases.replay: Click the green flag three times in a row. The ocean must be on screen from the very first instant, every single time.

clue.free: Re-read the ticket. The sea is not missing — it 'strolls in a second late'. So it does arrive. Watch the very first second again and say exactly what you see, in order.
clue.consult: Ask an agency that has CLOSED Case 04 — one question, detective to detective. First pair to reach it? Take HQ’s clue below — no shame in it.
clue.consultSolo: No other agencies are on shift today — you are the whole QA team. If re-reading the ticket didn’t crack it, go straight to HQ’s clue below.
clue.hq: Not a sprite at all — open the STAGE's scripts (click the Stage panel, bottom-right, beside the sprite list).

mechanicSteps: To change which backdrop a switch block shows: click the little white arrow on the block and pick from the list — the same move as Case 01's key menu.
To delete a block you do not want: drag it out of the script and drop it over the blocks list on the left. It disappears.
Careful — picking up a block also lifts every block joined UNDER it. Put the ones you want to keep back on the script first.

img.alt: A screenshot of the game: a plain white screen with the fish and the shark swimming on it, no ocean background.
img.caption: OceanOlivia's screenshot: fish swimming on a white screen.

stretchCase.name: The Jellyfish Job
stretchCase.ticket: Five stars, best shark game on the site — but NOTHING can hurt you! Where's the danger? Add something to dodge and it's perfect.
stretchCase.job: Add a Jellyfish from Scratch's sprite library: click 'Choose a Sprite' at the bottom right, then search 'Jellyfish'. Build it with the starter blocks in the picture below: the jellyfish drifts to a new spot every couple of seconds, and if the Shark ever touches it, the whole game stops. That 'if touching' block is next lesson's superpower — this is a sneak preview. Finished the jellyfish and want more? Design ONE more change of your own — a second danger, a speed-up, a power-up — and name it in your release note.
stretchCase.test: Click the green flag and dodge the jellyfish for twenty seconds… then swim into it ON PURPOSE. The game should freeze the instant you touch it.
stretchCase.confirm: Danger installed — touching the jellyfish ends the game
stretchCase.ask: One line for the release notes: what did you add, and what does it do to the player?
stretchCase.notePlaceholder: I added a jellyfish that... so now the player...
stretchCase.lockedNote: This tick unlocks when your release note above is written — a full sentence.

config.stretchNudge: Your fixed game has gone back to the players — but one five-star request is still pinned to the board. Take the job, or finish for today?

rc.title: The whole-game check
rc.text: You have fixed four bugs in one game — and some bugs only show up when the whole game is played. So before the game goes back to the players, QA plays the WHOLE game like a real player: one full minute, from the green flag to the end. Watch all four fixes holding at once:
watch: All four arrows — swim a full lap.
Eat at least five fish — the score counts every single one.
Fish keep arriving for the whole minute.
Restart twice — the ocean is there from the first instant, every time.
rc.confirm: Full sixty-second run — every fix held
rc.ask: There is no right or wrong number here — your count is simply proof you really played. How many fish did you catch in your full run?
rc.lockedNote: This button unlocks when you type the number of fish you caught into the box above.

ship.intro: When a games company sends a finished game out to its players, they call it SHIPPING the game. A fix only counts once the fixed game is saved somewhere safe — so ship tonight's game to your Drive:

steps.title: Save the fixed game
steps.text: In Scratch, open the File menu and choose 'Save to your computer'. The .sb3 lands in Downloads — that file IS your fixed game.

steps.title: Put it in your Drive
steps.text: Open drive.google.com, click into School, then DT Work, and drag the .sb3 in. The same folder as your micro:bit programs.

steps.title: Run the check
steps.text: The website looks in your Drive for a freshly-saved .sb3 — then the players get their game back.

config.boardTip: Lost your game? Nothing is broken — reload scratch.mit.edu, then File → Load from your computer, and pick the .sb3 again.
config.help: The board is your home screen. Its pins are: the film, Evidence Intake (where you get the broken game), the four cases, and the release desk where the fixed game goes back to the players. Start with Evidence Intake, then the TRAINING case. Inside a case you always do the same five things: see the bug happen, read the code, fix one thing, write your log, then re-play to prove it. Stuck on a case? Open the help steps on the card — re-reading the ticket is always free. Chapter 3 of the film is the one worth re-watching while you work.
introSteps: Play the broken game and SEE the bug happen with your own eyes.
Read the code and find the ONE thing that is wrong.
Fix that one thing in Scratch.
Write your CASE LOG — one sentence saying what was wrong and what you changed, just like the engineers wrote one sentence in their logbook in 1947.
Play the game again and WATCH the bug not happen. That re-play is your proof.
config.introAfter: When the log is written and the re-play is ticked, the case gets its CASE CLOSED stamp. Need help during a case? Every case card carries help steps: the first ones are free, but if you open the final clue from HQ — the company's head office — your stamp turns SILVER instead of GOLD. A silver case still counts. And remember: the website cannot see inside Scratch. YOU are the tester, so only tick what you truly watched happen.
config.logLead: Make your fix in Scratch. Then write your case log in the box just below — one sentence with two halves: **what was wrong**, and **what you changed**.
config.proofNote: This tick is a promise. It says: I played the game again, and I watched the bug NOT happen.
config.lockedNote: This stamp is locked until your case log in step 3 is written — both halves.
config.nudgeShort: Your log needs both halves in one sentence: what was wrong, and what you changed.
config.nudgeOwnWords: Say it in your OWN words — the grey line in the box is only a starter.
config.clueStep2Head: Help step 2 — ask another agency (another detective pair)
config.clueHqButton: Help step 3 — show HQ's clue (this case will then stamp SILVER instead of GOLD)
config.clueSilverNote: You took HQ's clue, so this case stamps SILVER when it closes. A silver case still counts — solve the next one without the clue for GOLD.
config.handbookNote: Come back to this film any time. Chapter 3 helps most while you are working on a case.
config.sealedNoKit: SEALED UNTIL YOU HAVE THE GAME
config.clueLadderCost: These help steps are FREE — your gold stamp is safe. Only step 3, HQ’s clue, turns this case’s stamp from GOLD to SILVER.

config.intro: Two questions about today before you go — and these ARE marked: your teacher sees your answers. Think like a detective, not a guesser.

items.stem: A sprite's script never runs when the green flag is clicked. What's the MOST likely reason?
options: There's no green-flag hat block on that script
The code is at the bottom of the workspace

items.stem: Your partner says: 'Fixed it! I saw one fish get eaten and the score moved.' What does a real QA tester do next?
options: Stamp it CASE CLOSED — it worked once
Re-play it and watch the fix work at least three times before closing the case
Delete the whole script and rebuild it, just to be safe
Add a few extra blocks so it definitely works

config.help: Two marked questions, answered on your own. You find out how you did at the end, after the last screen.

config.intro: Last one. You get five real blocks, and the sentence below describes the game's opening second. Two of the blocks are new, and they say what they do: hide makes the sprite invisible, show makes it visible again. Click the blocks into the order the sentence describes — you have spent the whole hour learning why order matters.

item.prompt: When the flag is clicked, the sprite gets into position without the player seeing it move, then appears in the middle of the screen and animates by changing costume forever.

config.help: Click blocks from the tray into your program, in the order the sentence describes. Check when you're sure — you'll be shown the working order if it's off.
config.doneText: Correct — that program does exactly what the card asked.

config.help: Click the button under each sentence that says how today really went, then the one that says how it felt. The comment box goes to your teacher and nobody else. Everyone finishes this screen before leaving.
